subject: Business
title: Pre-Mortem: Imagining Failure in Advance
description: A quick, practical guide to Pre-Mortem: Imagining Failure in Advance.

hook.text: Before launching, ask: 'Imagine this project failed spectacularly. Why?' The answers are gold.

buildup.text: Gary Klein developed the pre-mortem: assume failure has already happened and work backward to identify causes.

discovery.text: It overcomes groupthink by giving people permission to voice doubts they'd normally suppress.

twist.text: Post-mortems happen after damage is done. Pre-mortems prevent the damage before it starts.

climax.text: Teams that run pre-mortems identify 30% more potential risks than teams that use standard planning.

punchline.text: Imagine the worst before you start. Then build so it can't happen.

quiz.question: How does a pre-mortem differ from a post-mortem?
options: A pre-mortem imagines failure before launch; a post-mortem analyzes it after
A pre-mortem is less detailed than a post-mortem
Pre-mortems are only used in medicine

details.summary: A pre-mortem is a decision-making exercise where a team imagines a project has already failed and works backward to identify what caused the failure. Psychologist Gary Klein developed this technique to overcome optimism bias and groupthink that plague traditional planning processes.
details.whyItMatters: Teams naturally suppress doubts about plans they have invested effort in creating. Pre-mortems give explicit permission to voice concerns, surfacing risks that would otherwise remain hidden until they become actual problems during execution.
takeaways: Imagine the project has failed and work backward to identify why it happened
Pre-mortems overcome optimism bias by giving permission to identify weaknesses
Gary Klein's technique surfaces hidden risks that traditional planning misses

faq.question: How do you run an effective pre-mortem exercise?
faq.answer: After a plan is developed but before execution, tell the team to imagine it is one year later and the project has failed spectacularly. Each person independently writes reasons for the failure. Share and discuss all identified causes. Adjust the plan to address the most critical risks.

faq.question: Why is a pre-mortem more effective than simply asking what could go wrong?
faq.answer: Asking what could go wrong triggers defensive optimism in people invested in the plan. The pre-mortem frames failure as a certainty, psychologically freeing people to identify causes without feeling disloyal.
